problem: Consider the equation ${y}^{″}+12{y}^{′}+40y=0,$ where $y=y(x).$ If $y={e}^{\lambda x}$ is a solution, then $\lambda =$
worked_solution:
Assuming $y={e}^{\lambda x}$ and differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,{y}^{″}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}+12\lambda {e}^{\lambda x}+40{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}+12\lambda +40) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
{\lambda }^{2}+12\lambda +40=0
$$

The auxiliary equation can be solved by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+12\lambda +40 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}+12\lambda +36)-36+40 & =0 \\ (\lambda +6)^{2}+4 & =0 \\ (\lambda +6)^{2} & =-4 \\ \lambda +6 & =\pm 2\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =-6\pm 2\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,  $\lambda =-6\pm 2\text{i}$ are the complex roots of the auxiliary equation.
